paper_a.title: A Simple Proof of the Johnson--Lindenstrauss Extension Theorem

metadata.description: Both papers orbit the Johnson--Lindenstrauss (JL) phenomenon but address very different facets. Paper A proves the JL *extension* theorem (any Lipschitz map from an n-point subset of a metric space into Hilbert space extends to the whole superspace with Lipschitz constant blown up by O(sqrt(log n))) via a simple Gaussian + McShane argument. Paper B extends the classical JL *dimension-reduction* lemma from Euclidean space to non-Euclidean (pseudo-Euclidean / power-distance) settings, giving generalized JL transforms for arbitrary symmetric hollow dissimilarity matrices. The classical JL lemma appears in both as cited prior work (paper A cites it in a remark, paper B explicitly cites and extends it), so the genuine cross-paper match is at the level of the shared JL ancestor; paper-original contributions are largely disjoint.

matches.explanation: Both nodes refer to the original Johnson-Lindenstrauss 1984 dimension-reduction lemma. Paper A mentions it inside a remark explaining that the original JL extension proof relied on dimension reduction (the JL lemma); paper B states the lemma explicitly as cited prior work (PrP470.1) and uses it as the foundation it generalizes. Same underlying classical result; both treat it as external/folklore.

The JL *Extension* Theorem (paper A's main subject) is about extending a Lipschitz map from an n-point subset of a metric space to a Hilbert-valued map on the whole superspace, with Lipschitz blow-up O(sqrt(log n)). Paper B does not address Lipschitz extension at all -- its 'JL beyond Euclidean geometry' refers to dimension reduction in pseudo-Euclidean spaces, not extension theorems.

Definition of the Lipschitz constant of a metric-space mapping. Paper B's framework is built on bilinear forms / dissimilarity matrices and never invokes the Lipschitz-constant formalism, so this definition has no counterpart.

Equation bounding $\|U(x)-U(y)\|_{L_2(\Omega)}$ in terms of the expected max of squared standardized Gaussians indexed by pairs of points in T. This is internal to paper A's Gaussian-McShane proof of the extension theorem and has no analogue in paper B.

Gaussian maximum bound $\E[\max G_i^2]\lesssim \log m$ used as a key estimate in paper A's proof. Paper B's proofs use chi-square concentration on uniform-sphere Gaussians (PSP470.4), but the conceptual role and statement are different (concentration of a sum, not expected max), so this is not a meaningful alignment.
Paper A's main proof: a clever Gaussian-McShane argument for the JL extension theorem. Paper B has no extension-theorem proof to align it with.
Proof of the Gaussian-max bound via individual tail bound + union bound + tail integration. Paper B uses chi-square concentration in a different role; no direct counterpart.
Paper A's proof of the McShane extension theorem for finite domains via the inf-convolution formula $Q(x)=\min_{t\in T}q(t)+L d_X(x,t)$. Paper B has no extension construction.
Remark referencing Ball's extension theorem and Markov type 2; paper B does not touch this circle of ideas.

Definition of pseudo-Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^{p,q}$ and its $(p,q)$-bilinear form. Paper A works exclusively with Hilbert-valued (positive-definite) inner-product spaces; the pseudo-Euclidean / indefinite framework is unique to paper B.
$(p,q)$-norm and interval square in pseudo-Euclidean space. No counterpart in paper A.
Symmetric hollow dissimilarity matrix definition (no triangle inequality). Paper A only deals with metric spaces and Lipschitz maps; the notion of a non-metric dissimilarity matrix does not appear.
Gram matrix via centering for dissimilarity matrices. Specific to paper B's matrix-analytic setup.
Coordinate split $v^{(p)},v^{(q)}$ identifying Euclidean and pseudo-Euclidean parts. Paper A has no signature-based split.
Generalized power distance between weighted points. Paper A does not consider weighted points or power distances.
Unnormalized silhouette score between two Gaussians; paper-specific to paper B's appendix linking dissimilarities to Gaussian-cluster silhouettes. No analogue in paper A.
Pseudo-Euclidean representation of any symmetric hollow matrix. Paper-original to paper B; paper A's framework does not produce such representations.
Pseudo-Euclidean JL with additive Euclidean error (Lemma 2.2). Paper B's contribution; paper A has no JL-style dimension-reduction lemma.
Fine-grained JL lemma in pseudo-Euclidean space (Theorem 2.3). Paper B's main theorem; no counterpart in paper A.
Lemma 2.4 bounding the ratio of $(p,q)$-norm and Euclidean norm via CLT. No analogue in paper A.
Corollary 2.5 specializing the norm-ratio bound to uniform unit-sphere vectors. Specific to paper B.
Theorem 2.6: $(1\pm\varepsilon)$ JL distortion for random points in $(p,q)$-space. Paper B's main probabilistic JL result; no counterpart in paper A.
Lemma 3.1 expressing any symmetric hollow matrix as a power-distance matrix. Paper B's structural lemma; no analogue.
Lemma 3.2: JL for generalized power distance. Paper B contribution.
Theorem 3.3: power-distance JL lemma. Paper B's second main theorem; no counterpart.
Pseudo-Euclidean JL Transform algorithm. Paper A is purely existence-theoretic and contains no algorithm.
Power Distance JL Transform algorithm. Paper A contains no algorithm.
Problem statement: non-Euclidean dimensionality reduction from a dissimilarity matrix. Paper A is concerned with Lipschitz extension, not with dimensionality reduction or dissimilarity matrices.

Paper B's auxiliary equations: $(p,q)$-bilinear form, generalized power distance formula, coordinate recovery from Gram, silhouette-as-power-distance identity. None have analogues in paper A. Bundled in one entry for compactness.
